steps.prompt: I think of a number, double it and add $5$. I get $31$. What was my number, and how did you find it?
steps.placeholder: My number is… I found it by…

cards.title: New to this? Think of a number machine
cards.body: A number goes into a machine, the machine does some steps, and a number comes out. Working backwards means running the machine in reverse: start with what came out and undo each step, last step first. Every step has an opposite that undoes it: $+$ and $-$, $\times$ and $\div$, squaring and the square root. Four moves: (1) write the steps as a chain, like $n \to \times 2 \to +3 \to 17$; (2) start at the end; (3) undo the last step first, then the one before it; (4) check by running your answer forwards through the steps.

cards.title: Your first one: two steps back
cards.problem: Mia thinks of a number, adds $4$, then multiplies by $3$. She gets $27$. What was her number?

steps.text: Write the chain: $n \to +4 \to \times 3 \to 27$. Start at the end, $27$.
The last step was $\times 3$, so undo it first by dividing by $3$: $27 \div 3 = 9$.
Before that she added $4$. Undo it by subtracting $4$: $9 - 4 = 5$.
Check forwards: $5 + 4 = 9$ and $9 \times 3 = 27$ ✓. Her number is $5$.

cards.title: Worked example: undo the steps
cards.problem: Ravi thinks of a number, doubles it, adds $7$, then divides by $3$. He gets $9$. What was his number?

steps.text: Start at the end: $9$. The last step was dividing by $3$, so undo it first: $9 \times 3 = 27$.
Before that he added $7$. Undo it: $27 - 7 = 20$.
First he doubled. Undo it: $\frac{20}{2} = 10$. Check: $10 \to 20 \to 27 \to 9$. ✓

cards.title: Test the choices
cards.body: On a multiple-choice question the answer is one of the five choices, so you can put a choice into the problem and check it. How: (1) start with (C), the middle choice; (2) put it into the problem and work out the result; (3) compare with what the problem says; (4) if the result is too small, only (D) or (E) can work, and if it is too big, only (A) or (B); (5) try the next choice. Use it when an equation is hard to set up or solve but checking a number is quick.

cards.title: Worked example: test the choices
cards.problem: Three consecutive even numbers add up to $84$. What is the largest of them? (A) $24$ (B) $26$ (C) $28$ (D) $30$ (E) $32$

steps.text: Try (C), $28$: the numbers are $24$, $26$ and $28$, which add up to $78$. Too small, so the answer is (D) or (E).

try.prompt: What do $26$, $28$ and $30$ add up to?

steps.text: $26 + 28 + 30 = 84$ ✓, so the answer is (D). Two tries, and no equation needed.

cards.title: The common trap: undoing in the wrong order
cards.body: Undo the last step first, like taking off shoes before socks. If a number was doubled and then $4$ was added, subtract $4$ first and halve second. Halving first gives a different, wrong answer.

prompts: When would you test the choices instead of solving the problem directly?
